bridge: Builds on W11 object/property controls and W12 identity lifecycle. Use a fictional invoice service.
teaching:
Business rules constrain allowed transitions, not only reads. An invoice may be editable in draft but immutable after approval. The caller's role, object ownership and current state all matter at the moment the operation commits.

A hidden button and an unguessable identifier do not enforce a business rule. A server endpoint must check the current object under the authenticated principal. Apply the same invariant across web, API, bulk and background paths; one unprotected alternative can undermine the protected main screen.

Write a permission matrix before implementing branches. Include deny cases, but also ordinary owner actions and boundary states. For multi-step operations, use transaction/consistency mechanisms so a state change between check and update cannot authorise an invalid action.
example:
Policy: owner edits draft invoice only; reviewer approves; no one edits approved totals.
I1: owner A, draft, total 100
I2: owner B, approved, total 200
A edit I1 -> yes
A edit I2 -> no
B edit I2 -> no (state)
Reviewer approve I1 -> yes
Reviewer edit approved I2 -> no
explanation: B owns I2 but the approved-state invariant still denies editing. A reviewer role grants approval, not arbitrary alteration. These distinctions should be visible in the tests rather than encoded as “admin can do everything.”
exercise: Evaluate the five supplied cases and add an unauthenticated edit, an owner edit after concurrent approval and a bulk-edit endpoint containing I1/I2. State an explicit partial-versus-atomic bulk policy.
solution: The original five decisions are allow, deny, deny, allow, deny. No-identity edit is denied. If approval commits before the owner’s edit, the edit must see approved state and fail. For the bulk example choose all-or-nothing: A submits changes to I1 and I2; I2 fails owner/state checks, so neither change commits, including I1. A per-item-results policy could also be valid, but it must report each decision and preserve every item’s rules.
challenge: Propose server checks and transaction boundaries for approve-and-lock. Give a test where two requests race, and explain why checking only the initial page-load state is insufficient.
challenge_solution: Example paper schedule: editor reads I1 as draft; reviewer approves and locks I1; editor submits its old draft change. The server must check role, owner and current draft state at the protected update, so the edit fails after approval. Under a conditional-update design, the editor’s update includes state=draft and checks the affected-row count; approval changes draft→approved under the database’s selected transaction rules. If editing commits first, approval must deliberately approve that current version. Define version/locking policy rather than relying on the page’s old state.
